name: Aniam
title: Son of Shemida from the tribe of Manasseh
summary: Aniam appears in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:19 as one of four named sons of Shemida, a recognized patriarch in the tribe of Manasseh. Although he has no independent narrative in Scripture, his presence in the genealogy helps map the internal organization and branching of the tribe. The lineage of Shemida is linked to the land distribution under Joshua, where the clan received its own allotment in Canaan. Genealogical records like this serve an important function in biblical literature: they support the continuity of the tribes, anchor the people's identity in God's covenant promises, and reveal his faithfulness through successive generations.

keyEvents.title: Listed in the genealogy of Manasseh
keyEvents.description: Aniam is mentioned as one of the four sons of Shemida — along with Ahian, Shechem and Likhi — in the genealogical record of the tribe of Manasseh in 1 Chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Family lines of the tribe of Manasseh
keyEvents.description: Aniam is part of the detailed genealogical overview of the half-tribe of Manasseh, documenting the various branches and family structures of the tribe from the patriarchs through the conquest and settlement periods.

keyEvents.title: The inheritance of Shemida's clan in the promised land
keyEvents.description: As a descendant of Manasseh through Shemida, Aniam belonged to a clan that received land in Canaan during the allocation of territories, in accordance with God's promises to the people of Israel.

versions.summary: Aniam is a biblical figure who appears in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:19 as one of four sons of Shemida, a prominent patriarch within the tribe of Manasseh. Although Aniam has no independent narrative in the biblical texts, his place in the genealogy testifies to the structure and branching of the tribe of Manasseh. The lineage of Shemida traces back to the land distribution under Joshua, where Shemida is mentioned among those who received a portion of land. Such genealogies underscore the biblical emphasis on inheritance, belonging, and God's enduring care for the tribes of Israel.
versions.title: Son of Shemida from the tribe of Manasseh
versions.reason: [minor] Aniam appears in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles that was compiled after the exile, and his exact lifespan is unknown. 'Conquest' is reasonable given that Shemida is linked to the land distribution under Joshua, but there is some uncertainty. It can nevertheless be defended based on context.; [minor] The second key event ('Genealogies of the tribe of Manasseh') overlaps thematically with the first event. 'The people's complaint' is one interpretation, but others suggest 'I am the people's (portion)' or 'people of (my) spring'. The note could be nuanced somewhat further.

footnotes.text: The name Aniam (Hebrew: אֲנִיעָם) is composed of the elements 'ani' and 'am' (people). The interpretation is debated: it may mean 'the people's lament,' 'I am my people's [sorrow],' or possibly 'the people's source.' Such compound personal names in ancient Israel often reflected the family's circumstances or hopes at the time of birth.

Shemida, Aniam's father, is also mentioned in Numbers 26:32 as the head of the Shemidaites clan and in Joshua 17:2 as one of Manasseh's descendants who received a land allotment. This confirms the historical and tribal organizational significance of this lineage.

The genealogies in Chronicles were likely collected and edited after the Babylonian exile to restore Israel's national and religious identity. They serve to show God's faithful preservation of His people through generations, while also linking the post-exilic community to the promises made to their ancestors.

The tribe of Manasseh was unique in Israel because it was divided into two half-tribes: an eastern part that settled in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan, and a western part that received land in Canaan west of the Jordan (Joshua 17). This division reflects the tribe's size and historical development.

Archaeological findings from the central highlands of Canaan, which correspond to Manasseh's traditional tribal territory, show increased settlement during Iron Age I (c. 1200–1000 BCE), which may correspond with the tribe's establishment in the region.
